Protosilylation

title_content.content: Stable and Recyclable Copper Nanoclusters with Exposed Active Sites for Broad-Scope Protosilylation in Open Air

paragraph_content.content: Songwei Wen<sup>+</sup>, Chengkai Zhang<sup>+</sup>, Li-Juan Liu, Zhi Wang, Di Sun,* and Jian He*

Abstract: Despite recent advances in cluster-based catalysis for organic synthesis, the substrate scope of reactions catalyzed by metal nanoclusters is typically not superior to previously established catalytic systems. Herein, we develop new atomically precise copper nanoclusters for protosilylation, with scope expanding to alkenes and simple enynes that were not suitable for prior synthetic methodologies with traditional copper complexes. The involvement of a second copper center in the metal kernel during the migratory insertion step is thought to be responsible for the expanded scope. In addition, the reaction is highly compatible with water and can be carried out in open air rather than under inert gas protection. Mechanistic studies suggest that the cluster-catalyzed protosilylation proceeds in the absence of silyl radicals. The current findings demonstrate the potential of using metal nanoclusters for practical and sustainable chemical synthesis.

Because of the excellent tunability of ligand scaffolds and kernel structures, as well as the distinct photochemical characteristics of metal cores, atomically precise metal nanoclusters have shown promise as effective catalysts for the development of organic chemical processes.<sup>[1]</sup> In recent years, considerable efforts have been made toward constructing catalytically active copper nanoclusters in gram scales at low cost for sustainable synthetic applications<sup>[2]</sup> While several types of cluster-catalyzed coupling reactions can be achieved with increased efficiency,<sup>[3]</sup> developing robust copper nanocluster catalysts that can significantly broaden reaction scope when compared to established catalytic systems based on conventional copper complexes remains a major challenge.

On account of its flat structure and strong chelating effects, we anticipated that the incorporation of maleonitriledithiolate (mnt) in cluster synthesis would produce stable copper nanoclusters with exposed active sites suitable for practical catalytic applications.<sup>[4]</sup> The presence of Cu�Cu bonds in nanoclusters could have an important impact on the elementary steps during catalysis, potentially overcoming synthetic limitations in catalytic organic transformations. Since protosilylation reactions are crucial for organic synthesis<sup>[5]</sup> and can be facilitated by copper complexes,<sup>[6]</sup> investigating them with novel copper nanoclusters gave us an ideal opportunity to test the hypothesis. Even though copper-catalyzed protosilylation of alkynes and enynes with (dimethylphenylsilyl)boronic acid pinacol ester (pinB– SiMe Ph), a readily available and moisture-stable silylboronate, has been extensively studied through the use of various ligands (Schemes 1a and 1b),<sup>[7]</sup> there is still room for improvement in terms of catalyst turnover numbers (TONs) and reaction operability.

Here we report the synthesis and characterization of copper nanoclusters protected by mnt, thiolate, and bisphosphine ligands, which efficiently catalyze protosilylation of C�C multiple bonds under air atmosphere (Scheme 1c). The optimized nanocatalyst can be recycled multiple runs without loss of reactivity, and its remarkable stability is further demonstrated by UV–Vis, NMR, and ESI-MS studies. Aside from the high activity in gram-scale synthesis, the newly-developed copper nanocluster exhibits outstanding catalytic performance in the protosilylation of alkenes and enynes without the need for the pre-installation of electron-withdrawing functionalities.<sup>[7e,8]</sup> Additional interactions between the silyl group and the copper center adjacent to the exposed active site are likely to promote the key migratory insertion step, resulting in an expanded substrate scope in protosilylation reactions.

In a typical experiment, Cu nanoclusters protected by mnt ligands were synthesized using a simple method that consists of two major steps: (i) synthesizing stable copper(I) precursor under ambient conditions and (ii) introducing additional protective ligands to induce the formation of a Previous ligand-promoted protosilylation of alkynes

paragraph_content.content: Control experiments confirmed that both the catalyst and the base are necessary for the reaction to proceed (entries 2 and 3). In comparison to
\mathbf { C u } _ { 6 } { \cdot } 1 , \mathbf { C u } _ { 6 } { \cdot } 2

with less exposure to copper active sites displayed somewhat lower reactivity, providing product 1 in 85% yield (entry 4). Nevertheless, these two newly developed nanocatalysts are significantly superior to other copper nanoclusters in terms of promoting protosilylation (entries 5–7). The conventional copper complexes, including various Cu(I) and Cu(II) salts as well as their synthetic precursor
\mathrm { [ C u ( M e C N ) _ { 4 } ] B F _ { 4 } , }
proved to be far less effective than the cluster-based catalysts (entries 8–13). While weak organic bases (e.g.,
\mathrm { N E t } _ { 3 }
and 4-dimethylaminopyridine) are not as good as 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]- undec-7-ene (DBU), inorganic bases, such as

and NaO<sup>t</sup>Bu, also gave satisfactory results (entries 14 and 15). According to solvent studies, the involvement of protic solvents is crucial in the catalytic system (entries 18–20).

paragraph_content.content: Under the optimized reaction conditions, the alkyne substrates containing a variety of substituted aryl rings furnish the desired (E)-products with excellent levels of regioselectivity (Table 2, products 1–11). Both electrondonating and electron-withdrawing functional groups at different positions are well tolerated. Apart from phenylacetylene derivatives, alkyl-substituted terminal alkynes prove to be effective substrates in the protosilylation (Table 2, products 12 and 13), despite the relatively low regioselectivity for the substrate with a primary alkyl chain. Furthermore, under standard conditions, an
\alpha , \beta \mathrm { - }

unsaturated ester (14) is obtained with high levels of regio- and stereoselectivity. Trimethylsilylacetylene, a commonly used organosilicon compound, could be converted into a trans-1,2- disilylethene (15) with 88% yield. In addition, internal alkyne substrates are highly compatible with the clusterbased catalytic system (Table 2, products 16–18). Very importantly, the substrate scope can be further expanded to alkenes (Table 2, products 19 and 20), which was difficult to achieve in previous copper catalysis (Figure S5). For the synthesis of silyl-functionalized allenes, we broadened the substrate scope from 2-trifluoromethyl enynes to simple ones (Figure S6), giving desired di-substituted allenes 21 and 22 in yields of 71% and 78%, respectively.

paragraph_content.content: We have expanded our investigation on the functionalgroup compatibility of this synthetic method by conducting the template reaction in the presence of different additives (Table S7). Across a diverse array of additives such as aldehydes, ketones, nitriles, and various heterocycles, the cluster-catalyzed protosilylation proceeded with minimal or negligible influence on the yield of product 1. While an aniline displayed some incompatibility, it remained stable under the reaction conditions. In contrast, although the protosilylation proceeded effectively in the presence of a phenol or an N-methyl pyrrole, these two additives exhibited poor recovery.

Notably, the gram-scale reaction can proceed smoothly with a 20-fold lower catalyst loading, providing a TON as high as 14200 (eq. 1). To demonstrate the synthetic utility of this protosilylation, we subjected product 1 to a range of coupling and hydrogenation conditions for the construction of carbon�carbon and carbon–heteroatom bonds (Scheme 2). A number of functionalized trans-olefins, including high value-added bromoalkene 26 and diene 28, were synthesized in high yields. When an electron-deficient aryl group was introduced to the alkyne terminal of the enyne, a second protosilylation reaction occurred in the resulting di-substitute allene,<sup>[13]</sup> activating the double bond closer to the aromatic ring (eq. 2). The other silyl group approached the central carbon atom of the allene from the opposite direction as the previously installed silyl group, giving disilylated product 33 in the (E)-configuration, most likely through a migratory insertion pathway.

Due to the high compatibility with air atmosphere and the lack of influence from (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxy (TEMPO), a well-established radical trapping reagent (Figure 3c), we concluded that the protosilylation pathway involving a silyl radical intermediate<sup>[14]</sup> is highly unlikely, which clearly differs from cluster-based catalysis for protoborylation.<sup>[15]</sup> Since a mixed-solvent strategy was employed in the reaction optimization, we examined the proton source in the catalytic system with the corresponding deuterated solvents (Figure 3d). When acetonitrile-

was utilized instead of acetonitrile, no deuterated product formed. The deuterium ratio of
\mathrm { D _ { a } }
near the aromatic substituent increased to 67% and 77%, when the reaction was carried out under air and nitrogen atmospheres, respectively. The unexpected deuteration of
\mathrm { D } _ { \mathrm { b } } .

\mathbf { D _ { a } }
and
\mathrm { { D _ { b } } }
under nitrogen atmosphere suggested that water in the reaction mixture could possibly contribute to the protonation steps.

Based on the experimental results and DFT calculations, we proposed a plausible catalytic cycle in Figure 3e. With the aid of the base and methanol, the exposed active site on the copper nanocluster undergoes ligand association to generate cluster–silyl intermediate A. Following the side-on binding of an alkyne molecule through transition state TS-1, intermediate B forms with a <sup>t</sup>BuS ligand dissociated from the copper active center. In the subsequent silyl migration step, 1,2-insertion occurs with an additional stabilization effect from the nearby copper center, resulting in the highest activation energy of only 23.1 kcal mol<sup>–1</sup>. Because of this unique migratory insertion mode involving two copper centers of TS-2, the catalytic protosilylation proceeds smoothly at room temperature, with an extended substrate scope that includes
\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C }
double bonds. Furthermore, the concerted insertion leads to the formation of intermediate
\mathbf { C } ,
in which the cluster unit and the silyl group are cis to each other. Therefore, deprotonation of C with methanol yields a trans-alkene and intermediate D. The initial cluster catalyst
is regenerated via ligand dissociation in the presence of a conjugate acid.
We present here the development of mnt ligand-protected
\mathrm { C u } _ { 6 }

nanoclusters with exposed active sites for efficiently catalyzing protosilylation reactions under ambient conditions, with a TON of up to 14200. The nanocatalyst can be recycled at least 8 runs and is applicable to gram-scale synthesis. Apart from its high reactivity with alkyne substrates, the
\mathrm { C u } _ { 6 }

nanocluster can also be employed to functionalize alkenes and simple enynes. The new migratory insertion mode based on two copper centers in the cluster kernel provides guidance for the future design of catalytically active metal nanoclusters to transform synthetic methodologies.
